note: Hand-authored example on synthetic work. Not output from a live API run.
task: Get approval for a two-week pilot

plan.purpose: Help the head of operations approve or reject a bounded experiment
plan.audience: Head of operations and three team leads
plan.stakes: Wasted time, unnecessary spending, and a premature company-wide rollout
plan.qualityBar: A feasible two-week pilot, a specific decision request, and a way to judge improvement
assumptions: The brief's no-new-software-budget constraint applies to this proposal

lenses.name: Decision and feasibility
lenses.why: The reader needs an approvable action, not another discussion
lenses.evidenceNeeded: Supplied memo and brief; no measured meeting outcomes
checks: Does it respect the existing-tools constraint?
Can the reader tell what success would mean?

outOfScope: Verifying team complaints or tool pricing
Proving the pilot will save time
plan.stopWhen: The reader can decide on a feasible pilot and evaluate time and decision quality

limitations: Synthetic, hand-authored illustration; not a live model run
No external facts or real outcomes verified

review.verdict: The core idea is concrete, but this draft asks for the wrong commitment. Make it an existing-tools pilot with a decision request and a success criterion before sending.

findings.title: A company-wide purchase is not the pilot the brief calls for

evidence.detail: I propose buying a new collaboration tool and rolling it out to every team.

findings.why: The head of operations must either reject the spending or reopen scope before considering the meeting experiment.
findings.action: Propose a two-week experiment with one team using the current shared document. Keep any software purchase out of this decision.
findings.verify: Can the reader approve the pilot without approving new spend or a wider rollout?

findings.title: The final line defers the decision
findings.why: The intended next action is pilot approval; the close creates another meeting instead of making that choice legible.
findings.action: Close with an explicit approve-or-reject request and state which owner and team still need confirmation.
findings.verify: Ask a reader what decision is being requested. They should identify the pilot, not another discussion.

findings.title: The proposal cannot distinguish a shorter meeting from a better meeting

evidence.detail: The meeting feels slow. Several people have complained.

findings.why: Subjective frustration establishes a reason to investigate, not whether cutting meeting time preserves decision quality.
findings.action: Before the pilot, establish a baseline and propose tracking both time and missed or deferred decisions. Do not invent measurements.
findings.verify: After two weeks, compare time and decision quality before recommending broader adoption.

preserve.point: Keep the specific 60-to-25-minute hypothesis; it gives the pilot a concrete change to test.

evidence.detail: We should shorten the weekly planning meeting from 60 minutes to 25 minutes.

unknowns: Whether 25 minutes is enough for this team's decisions
Actual meeting costs and missed decisions
Human outcome validation is still needed
